reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: A benign, slow-growing, vascular tumour (paraganglioma) arising from paraganglionic tissue on the promontory of the middle ear
The classic presentation is pulsatile tinnitus synchronous with the heartbeat, together with conductive hearing loss
Otoscopy shows a reddish mass behind the tympanic membrane, often described as a rising-sun appearance, that may blanch on positive pneumatic pressure (Brown sign)
It should be distinguished from glomus jugulare, which arises around the jugular bulb and tends to involve the skull base and lower cranial nerves
Imaging is essential to define the tumour and separate a confined tympanic lesion from more extensive jugulare or vagale disease
Biopsy through the eardrum is avoided because these lesions are vascular and bleed readily
Treatment of a confined glomus tympanicum is usually surgical excision, which is generally curative for small lesions
A small proportion of paragangliomas are catecholamine-secreting or part of a familial syndrome, so relevant clinical features should prompt further evaluation
reference.pathophysiology: Glomus tympanicum is a paraganglioma derived from paraganglion cells associated with the tympanic branches of the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves along the cochlear promontory. These tumours are highly vascular, composed of nests of chief cells in a rich capillary network, and grow slowly to fill the middle-ear cleft, impairing ossicular movement and producing conductive hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus. Although almost always benign and non-secretory, a minority of paragangliomas produce catecholamines or occur within hereditary syndromes such as those linked to succinate dehydrogenase gene mutations, and multicentric tumours can occur.
additionalDifferentials: Aberrant internal carotid artery in the middle ear
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy and microscopy to identify the retrotympanic vascular mass
High-resolution computed tomography of the temporal bone to define the tumour and assess the jugular bulb and bony margins
Magnetic resonance imaging with contrast to characterise soft-tissue extent and distinguish from a glomus jugulare
Angiography and preoperative embolisation for larger or vascular lesions
Screening for catecholamine secretion and family history where a functional or hereditary paraganglioma is suspected
redFlags: A pulsatile retrotympanic mass that should never be biopsied blindly through the eardrum because of brisk bleeding
Extension to the skull base or lower cranial nerve palsies suggesting glomus jugulare rather than a confined tympanicum
Symptoms of catecholamine excess indicating a functional (secreting) paraganglioma
Multicentric tumours or a strong family history suggesting a hereditary paraganglioma syndrome
reference.prognosis: As a benign, slow-growing tumour, a glomus tympanicum confined to the middle ear has an excellent outlook with complete surgical excision, which is usually curative; larger or jugulare lesions are more challenging and carry greater risk to hearing and cranial nerves.
pitfalls: Biopsying a vascular middle-ear mass through the tympanic membrane and causing significant haemorrhage
Mistaking an aberrant carotid artery or high jugular bulb for a tumour
Failing to image adequately and underestimating a glomus jugulare with skull-base extension
Overlooking a secreting or hereditary paraganglioma
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Complete surgical excision, most often transcanal or via tympanotomy, is curative for disease confined to the middle ear
Radiotherapy or stereotactic radiosurgery as an alternative for tumour control in poor surgical candidates
Observation with serial imaging for small, minimally symptomatic tumours in older patients
Avoid transtympanic biopsy because these lesions are vascular and bleed readily, and consider preoperative embolisation for larger tumours
Screen for catecholamine secretion where a functional or hereditary paraganglioma is suspected
Offer genetic evaluation for succinate dehydrogenase mutations and screen for multicentric disease
Manage through an ENT and skull base team, with imaging to distinguish a confined tympanicum from jugulare or vagale disease
